g.text: The window lifecycle — assign, merge, group and trigger, accumulate and collect
2 of key "b"'s arrivals merge · 5 state entries · the straggler beats collection by 1 event
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
STEP 1 OF 4 — ASSIGN
one event, three windowings, three different assignments
fixed: id 4 (et 12:04:05)
sliding: the same event
session: the same event
1 window, whose BOUNDS are not known yet
what assign reads
e.et and the windowing function — never the arrival time
The session row is the odd one: an event is assigned to a session whose START and END are still provisional, because a later event can extend
either.
That is the whole reason the next step exists. Fixed and sliding assignments are final at assign time; session assignments are not.
Step 1/4 — ASSIGN — by event time, and possibly to several windows
Assign reads `e.et` and the windowing rule, and nothing else. For fixed and sliding that settles the question permanently. For a session it does
not: id 4 joins a session whose bounds depend on events that have not arrived — so a session assignment is a hypothesis, and the merge step is
what revises it.
The window lifecycle — assign, merge, group and trigger, accumulate and collect
2 of key "b"'s arrivals merge · 5 state entries · the straggler beats collection by 1 event
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
STEP 2 OF 4 — MERGE (key "b", in processing order)
id 2 arrives (et 12:01:30)
new session
id 5 arrives (et 12:04:20)
new session
id 6 arrives (et 12:03:40)
MERGED into a session
id 7 arrives (et 12:00:50)
MERGED into a session
2 of key "b"'s 4 arrivals merge: id 6 and id 7 each arrive OUT OF ORDER and extend a session backwards.
Note what that means: a session's START moved after the session existed. No other windowing has a boundary that can change.
Step 2/4 — MERGE — a later arrival can absorb an existing session
Watch the second column change shape as events arrive. id 6 (et 12:03:40) arrives after a later event and pulls a session's start backwards; id 7
does the same to the other one. Merging is what makes sessions dynamic — and it is also why a session's value can change after it has been
reported.
The window lifecycle — assign, merge, group and trigger, accumulate and collect
2 of key "b"'s arrivals merge · 5 state entries · the straggler beats collection by 1 event
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
STEP 3 OF 4 — GROUP BY (KEY, WINDOW), THEN TRIGGER
one state entry per (key, window) pair — the unit everything downstream works on
watermark passes 12:02:03 at event 4
watermark passes 12:06:05 at event 8
never collected in this stream
watermark passes 12:03:30 at event 8
watermark passes 12:06:20 at event 8
There are 5 state entries here, one per (key, session). The number of them is data-dependent, which fixed windows never are.
1 of them is never collected in this stream, so its memory is held until the job ends.
Step 3/4 — GROUP and TRIGGER — state per (key, window)
The unit of streaming state is the (key, window) pair, and for sessions the NUMBER of those pairs depends on the data. 5 entries here; a quieter
stream would give fewer and a burstier one more. That is the practical difference between sessions and fixed windows: you cannot size the state in
advance.
The window lifecycle — assign, merge, group and trigger, accumulate and collect
2 of key "b"'s arrivals merge · 5 state entries · the straggler beats collection by 1 event
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · gap 120s · 5 sessions
STEP 4 OF 4 — ACCUMULATE, THEN COLLECT
collection is a watermark event, and it is what bounds the memory
a session is NOT done when it looks idle
idleness is a fact about arrivals, not about event time
it is done when the watermark passes end + gap
for key "b"'s session holding id 7: 12:03:30
that happens at event 8
and id 7 arrived at event 7 — 1 event earlier
so at gap 120s no retraction is needed
the straggler landed before its session was collected
The margin is 1 event. Shrink the gap to 40s and the same session is collected at event 4 while id 7 arrives at event 7 — and a retraction
becomes mandatory.
So "does this pipeline need retractions?" is not answerable from the data alone. It depends on the gap, and here it turns on a single event.
Step 4/4 — ACCUMULATE and GARBAGE-COLLECT — on the watermark
The lifecycle ends where the memory does: a session's state is released when the watermark passes its end plus the gap. In this stream, at gap
120s, that happens 1 event AFTER the straggler arrives — so nothing has to be retracted. At gap 40s the order flips and a retraction is forced.
The next concept follows that case all the way through.
